questions.q: What is partial failure?
questions.explain: In one process a call returns or throws. Across machines, payments may have charged the card while its reply was lost, so the caller sees a failure for work that happened. That uncertainty is what distributed designs are built around.
options: A request that returns half of its data
Some parts of a system work while others do not, and a caller often cannot tell which parts did their work
A server that restarts itself after a crash
A database transaction that commits some rows and not others

questions.q: Orders called payments and timed out after 200 ms. What does orders know?
questions.explain: All of those worlds look the same from the caller: silence. The safe responses are to retry with an idempotency key, or to ask payments later what happened to that key.
options: The card was not charged
The card was charged, but the reply was slow
Nothing about the charge: the request may have been lost, the reply may have been lost, or payments may still be working on it
Payments has crashed

questions.q: Which delivery guarantee can you build over a network that loses and duplicates messages?
questions.explain: Retries make sure a message gets through, and create duplicates. Remembering processed ids makes the duplicates harmless. "Exactly once" in product documentation usually means exactly this pair.
options: Exactly once, by using TCP
At least once (retry until acknowledged) plus deduplication by message id, which gives effectively-once processing
Exactly once, by sending every message twice
At most once, which never loses messages

questions.q: Why does the simulator draw its random numbers from a seeded generator instead of Math.random()?
questions.explain: A test that fails once in a hundred runs and cannot be reproduced teaches nothing. With a seed, the failing run is a number you can paste into a bug report. (Seeded generators like mulberry32 are not safe for cryptography; use crypto for secrets.)
options: Seeded numbers are more random
Math.random() does not work in the browser
The same seed gives the same sequence, so a run (including a failure) can be repeated exactly, on any machine
Seeded generators are required for cryptography

questions.q: What is the main benefit of running the network in simulated time (a discrete-event simulation)?
questions.explain: The simulator keeps a timeline sorted by simulated time and jumps from event to event. A 5-second outage takes no real time to test, and two runs never disagree because of a slow machine.
options: It makes real network calls faster
Nothing actually waits, so thousands of round trips run in milliseconds, and timings are exact and repeatable
It removes the need for timeouts
It lets messages travel faster than light

questions.q: A payments server pauses for 450 ms (a garbage-collection pause) and the failure detector, with a 250 ms timeout, declares it dead. What is this, and why is it dangerous?
questions.explain: A slow node and a dead node send the same thing: nothing. Systems must survive a node that was wrongly declared dead, for example with leases and fencing tokens that make the old owner's late writes fail.
options: A true positive; nothing is dangerous about it
A false positive: if a replacement takes over and the old server then wakes up and finishes its work, two servers may do the same work
A network partition, which CAP says cannot happen
A clock skew problem

questions.q: You lower a failure detector's timeout from 600 ms to 250 ms. What changes?
questions.explain: No timeout is both fast and never wrong. Pick it from measured latencies and pauses, and often require several missed heartbeats before acting.
options: Crashes are detected later, and false alarms become rarer
Crashes are detected sooner, and false alarms (live but slow nodes declared dead) become more likely
Nothing, because heartbeats are sent every 100 ms either way
The detector becomes exact

questions.q: Ada's second address change was stamped with an earlier time than her first, and last-write-wins kept the old address. What caused it?
questions.explain: Clock skew between machines is normal. Last-write-wins with wall clocks silently discards whichever write happens to carry the smaller stamp. Use a version from one authority, or a logical clock.
options: The replicas applied the writes in the wrong order
The server that took the second write had a clock two seconds slow; wall-clock stamps from different machines cannot order writes closer together than the skew
JavaScript's Date.now() has only one-second precision
The network lost the second write

questions.q: Which clock should you use to measure how long a request took, or to implement a deadline?
questions.explain: A wall clock can be stepped backwards or forwards by NTP, which makes durations negative and deadlines fire at the wrong time. A monotonic clock counts elapsed time only.
options: Date.now(), because it is the time of day
A monotonic clock such as performance.now(), which only moves forward and is never adjusted
A Lamport clock
The database's now()

questions.q: A service whose Lamport clock is at 4 receives a message stamped 9. What is the time of the receive event?
questions.explain: On receive: take the maximum of your clock and the message's stamp, then count the event: max(4, 9) + 1 = 10. That jump is what makes every effect's time larger than its cause's.

questions.q: Event A has Lamport time 3 and event B has Lamport time 7. What can you conclude?
questions.explain: Lamport clocks guarantee one direction only: if A happened before B, then time(A) < time(B). A smaller number does not prove causality. To tell "before" from "concurrent", you need vector clocks.
options: A happened before B
B did not happen before A; but A and B may be concurrent
A and B are concurrent
A happened 4 ms before B

questions.q: What can vector clocks tell you that Lamport clocks cannot?
questions.explain: A vector clock keeps one counter per node. If each clock is ahead in some entry, the events were concurrent, like Ada's two offline cart edits, and must be merged instead of one winning.
options: The exact wall-clock time of each event
Whether two events were concurrent, so neither should silently overwrite the other
Which server is the leader
How long a message took to arrive

questions.q: Ada saves a new address, reloads the page, and sees her old address. Which consistency guarantee was violated?
questions.explain: Her read went to a follower that had not received her write yet. A session guarantee (remember the version you wrote, skip replicas that are behind) fixes exactly this, without making every read go to the leader.
options: Linearizability of the leader
Read-your-writes
Partition tolerance
Monotonic clocks

questions.q: An order page shows "shipped", and on the next refresh shows "paid" again. Which guarantee was violated?
questions.explain: The two refreshes were served by replicas with different lag. Eventual consistency allows this; the monotonic-reads session guarantee forbids it by never accepting a version older than one already seen.
options: Read-your-writes
Monotonic reads: a client saw older data after newer data
Eventual consistency
Causal delivery of heartbeats

questions.q: What does eventual consistency promise?
questions.explain: It is the weakest useful promise: no bound on staleness and no ordering between clients. It is fine for view counters and recommendations, and dangerous for stock and money.
options: Every read returns the latest write
Replicas agree within 100 ms
If writes stop, all replicas eventually return the same value; before that, reads may be stale
Writes are applied in the order the clients sent them

questions.q: What does the CAP theorem actually say?
questions.explain: Partitions happen whether you choose them or not, so the real choice is what each operation does while one lasts. Outside partitions, both can hold, although consistency still costs latency (PACELC).
options: A system can only ever have two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance
During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between answering every request (availability) and every read seeing the latest write (consistency)
Consistent systems are always slower than available ones
Partitions can be prevented with enough bandwidth

questions.q: During a partition, which ShopFlow operation should prefer consistency (and sometimes answer "try again")?
questions.explain: Selling stock that does not exist costs refunds and trust, so a clear error is better. Recommendations, counters and carts can be stale or merged later, so they stay available.
options: Showing the "customers also bought" list
Counting product page views
Selling the last bag of rice in stock
Adding an item to a shopping cart

questions.q: With 3 replicas, writes wait for 2 confirmations (W = 2) and reads ask 2 replicas (R = 2). Why does every read see the latest confirmed write?
questions.explain: Overlapping quorums guarantee that at least one replica in every read set has the newest write. With one replica down, both reads and writes still find 2 replicas.
options: Because the leader answers every read
Because R + W > N: any 2 replicas asked for a read share at least one replica with any 2 that confirmed the write, and the read keeps the highest version
Because replication lag is zero
Because two replicas never fail at the same time

questions.q: There is no partition. Why is a write that waits for a majority of replicas still a trade-off?
questions.explain: PACELC extends CAP: under a Partition choose Availability or Consistency, Else choose Latency or Consistency. Most of the time you are paying the second price, not the first.
options: It is not; without a partition consistency is free
Waiting for replicas in other places makes every write slower than writing to the nearest one: consistency costs latency (the "else" part of PACELC)
Majorities can only be reached during a partition
It uses more disk space

questions.q: A payments instance crashed, but for several seconds the registry still lists it and clients keep calling it. Why?
questions.explain: Discovery learns about crashes the same way a failure detector does: by silence, after a delay. Shorter TTLs shrink the window; timeouts and retries on another instance cover what remains.
options: The registry has a bug
A crashed instance cannot deregister itself; its entry only disappears when its TTL expires without a heartbeat
Clients cache DNS forever
The instance is still healthy

questions.q: In server-side service discovery, who picks the instance that handles a request?
questions.explain: Kubernetes Services, DNS names behind a load balancer and service meshes work this way, so application code rarely talks to a registry. Client-side discovery puts the lookup and the choice in the caller instead.
options: The calling service, after asking the registry
A load balancer or proxy in front of the service; the caller only knows one stable name
The database
The instance with the lowest Lamport time

questions.q: A seed sweep reports "charged twice in 237 of 500 runs, first failing seed 1". What is the most useful thing about that report?
questions.explain: The percentage depends on the simulated fault rates, not on production. The seed is the valuable part: a rare, timing-dependent bug turned into a repeatable test.
options: It proves the naive design fails exactly 47.4% of the time in production
Seed 1 reproduces one failing history exactly, every time, so you can debug it and keep it as a regression test
It shows that seed 1 is a bad seed that should be avoided
It means the network simulator is broken

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A seeded generator is a pure function of its seed: the same seed always gives the same sequence, and a different seed a different one. That is what makes simulated failures repeatable.
options: true false
false false
true true
false true

questions.q: A tiny discrete-event timeline. What does it print?
questions.explain: Events run in order of simulated time; two events at the same time run in the order they were scheduled. Here the reply wins the tie with the timeout, which is exactly the kind of race a real system resolves by luck.
options: 0:request sent | 10:heartbeat | 30:reply from payments | 30:timeout fires
0:request sent | 10:heartbeat | 30:timeout fires | 30:reply from payments
30:reply from payments | 10:heartbeat | 30:timeout fires | 0:request sent
0:request sent | 30:reply from payments | 10:heartbeat | 30:timeout fires

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Payments was already at 2, so receiving a message stamped 1 gives max(2, 1) + 1 = 3. Its reply is 4, and orders jumps from 1 to max(1, 4) + 1 = 5. Every receive is later than its send, and a clock never moves backwards.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first pair differs only in Abuja's counter, which is smaller in the first clock. In the second, Lagos is ahead in one and Abuja in the other (a missing entry counts as 0), so neither happened before the other. Key order does not matter.
options: before concurrent equal
before after equal
concurrent concurrent equal
before concurrent concurrent

questions.q: Two servers stamp writes with their own clocks. What does this print?
questions.explain: Kano's clock runs 2.5 seconds fast, so its write at real time 4000 is stamped 6500, higher than every Lagos stamp. Last-write-wins keeps the oldest price. The skew is larger than the gap between the writes, and nothing reports the loss.
options: price ₦72,000 | price ₦74,000
price ₦74,000 | price ₦74,000
price ₦75,000 | price ₦74,000
price ₦72,000 | price ₦72,000

questions.q: A consumer receives messages from an at-least-once network. What does this print?
questions.explain: Seven deliveries, four distinct messages, four charges. Deduplicating by message id turns at-least-once delivery into effectively-once processing.

questions.q: A receiver processes messages strictly in sequence, holding back early ones. What does this print?
questions.explain: 2 waits for 1, then both go; 4 waits for 3 (its duplicate is absorbed by the Set), then 3 and 4 go; 6 waits for 5, which has not arrived. With loss, 5 might never arrive, which is why real protocols add acknowledgements and resends.
options: 1,2,3,4 waiting: 6
2,1,4,3,6 waiting:
1,2,3,4,6 waiting:
1,2,4,3 waiting: 6

questions.q: Heartbeats from payments arrived at these times. The monitor checks every 100 ms and suspects the node when nothing arrived for more than 250 ms. What does this print?
questions.explain: After the heartbeat at 400, the first check with a gap above 250 ms is at 700 (a gap of 300). The heartbeat at 900 clears it. After 1100 the node goes quiet, and at 1400 the gap is 300 again. Whether the silence was a pause or a crash, the detector cannot know.
options: suspect at 700, alive at 900, suspect at 1400
suspect at 500, alive at 900, suspect at 1200
suspect at 700, suspect at 1400
suspect at 600, alive at 900, suspect at 1300

questions.q: With N = 3 replicas, count the (write set, read set) pairs that share no replica, for two configurations. What does this print?
questions.explain: With R + W = 4 > 3, every read set overlaps every write set. With R = 1, a read can land on the one replica the write skipped: for each of the 3 possible write sets there is exactly one such replica, so 3 of the 9 pairs miss the write and may return stale data.
options: W=2 R=2: 0 misses, W=2 R=1: 3 misses
W=2 R=2: 0 misses, W=2 R=1: 0 misses
W=2 R=2: 3 misses, W=2 R=1: 0 misses
W=2 R=2: 1 misses, W=2 R=1: 6 misses

questions.q: A client reads with a session guarantee. What does this print?
questions.explain: The client has already seen version 4, so follower-2 at version 3 is skipped in favour of the leader, twice. Follower-1 is up to date and can answer. The client never goes back in time and the leader only serves the reads that need it.
options: leader@v5 follower-1@v5 leader@v5
follower-2@v3 follower-1@v5 follower-2@v3
leader@v5 leader@v5 leader@v5
follower-2@v3 follower-1@v5 leader@v5

questions.q: Five replicas are split by a partition into two groups. Each side accepts a write only if it can reach a majority. What does this print?
questions.explain: A majority of 5 is 3. At most one side of a partition can have it, so two sides can never both accept conflicting writes. When r3 is also unreachable, nobody has a majority, and a CP system refuses writes everywhere: that is the availability it gives up.
options:
lagos: accepts writes, abuja: 503
lagos: 503, abuja: 503

lagos: accepts writes, abuja: accepts writes
lagos: accepts writes, abuja: accepts writes

lagos: accepts writes, abuja: 503
lagos: accepts writes, abuja: 503

lagos: 503, abuja: 503
lagos: 503, abuja: 503

questions.q: Write a LamportClock class with tick() (a local event: add one and return the time), send() (sending is an event: same as tick) and receive(remote) (set the time to the larger of the local time and remote, then count the event and return it).
questions.explain: Shipping was already at 3, so a message stamped 1 does not move it back: max(3, 1) + 1 = 4. Orders jumps from 1 to max(1, 10) + 1 = 11. The clock never goes backwards.

questions.q: Write compare(a, b) for vector clocks (objects mapping node names to counters; a missing node counts as 0). Return "before" if a is less than or equal to b everywhere and less somewhere, "after" for the opposite, "equal", or "concurrent" when each is ahead somewhere.
questions.explain: Look at every node that appears in either clock, and treat missing entries as 0; otherwise { laptop: 0 } and {} would look different although they describe the same history.

questions.q: When a node receives a vector clock, it merges it into its own: take the maximum of each entry, then add one to its own entry. Write receive(own, remote, self) that returns the new clock as a new object, without changing own.
questions.explain: The element-wise maximum records everything either side has seen; the increment records the receive itself. The merged clock is now "after" both inputs, which is exactly what receiving a message means.

questions.q: Write quorumRead(replies, r). replies holds the answers that arrived before the deadline, each { replica, version, value }. If fewer than r replies arrived, throw Error("no quorum: X of R"). Otherwise return the value with the highest version.
questions.explain: Pick by version, never by arrival order: the fastest replica is often the most stale. Refusing to answer without a quorum is the "C" choice of CAP: an honest error instead of a possibly stale value.

questions.q: Write describe(n, w, r) returning a string: "consistent" or "may be stale" (consistent when r + w > n), then how many replicas may be down while writes still work (n - w) and while reads still work (n - r), in the format shown.
questions.explain: The last two lines show the trade-off: W = R = 1 is fast and very available but stale; W = 5, R = 1 gives cheap consistent reads, and a single down replica stops every write.
questions.expected:
N=3 W=2 R=2: consistent, writes survive 1 down, reads survive 1 down
N=5 W=3 R=3: consistent, writes survive 2 down, reads survive 2 down
N=5 W=1 R=1: may be stale, writes survive 4 down, reads survive 4 down
N=5 W=5 R=1: consistent, writes survive 0 down, reads survive 4 down

questions.q: Write inOrder(arrivals): messages are numbered from 1, may arrive in any order and more than once. Return the list of numbers in the order a receiver can process them, each exactly once, never skipping a number that has not arrived yet.
questions.explain: 7 is held back because 6 never arrived, and without 1 nothing can be processed at all. Holding back is correct, and it is also why a lost message stalls an ordered stream until it is resent.

questions.q: Write healthy(lastHeartbeat, now, ttl): lastHeartbeat maps instance names to the time of their last heartbeat. Return the names whose last heartbeat is at most ttl ms before now, sorted.
questions.explain: With a long TTL, payments-2, silent for 5.2 seconds, is still listed and will receive requests. With a short TTL and no fresh heartbeats, every instance drops out, which is why TTLs must be comfortably longer than the heartbeat interval.
